# Plantain

<section class="hmi-quick-read" id="plantain-quick-read" data-hmi-quick-read aria-labelledby="plantain-quick-read-label"><div class="hmi-quick-read-label" id="plantain-quick-read-label">Quick read</div>

Most monitored plantain is low in metals, but lead is the one to check: plantain grown beside mining-polluted rivers in Ghana averaged about 1,000 µg/kg, far above the 100 µg/kg fruit limit.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops|2]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Adjei-Mensah R, Ofori H, Tortoe C, Johnson PT, Aryee D, Frimpong SK · 2021</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops">Effect of home processing methods on the levels of heavy metal contaminants in four food crops grown in and around two mining towns in Ghana</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Toxicology Reports 8 (2021) 1830–1838</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/eu-2023-915-contaminants-maximum-levels|3]]<span href="../sources/eu-2023-915-contaminants-maximum-levels">Commission Regulation (EU) 2023/915 of 25 April 2023 on maximum levels for certain contaminants in food and repealing Regulation (EC) No 1881/2006</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Official Journal of the European Union</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/eu-2023-915-contaminants-maximum-levels">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

<ul>
<li>
<strong>Metals of concern:</strong>

Lead decides most plantain questions; mercury matters near gold mining, and nickel is high wherever measured.<sup class="cite">[[sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops|2]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Adjei-Mensah R, Ofori H, Tortoe C, Johnson PT, Aryee D, Frimpong SK · 2021</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops">Effect of home processing methods on the levels of heavy metal contaminants in four food crops grown in and around two mining towns in Ghana</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Toxicology Reports 8 (2021) 1830–1838</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/borteysam2015-tarkwa-cassava-plantain-soil-metals|4]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Bortey-Sam N, Nakayama SMM, Akoto O, Ikenaka Y, Fobil JN, Baidoo E, Mizukawa H, Ishizuka M · 2015</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/borteysam2015-tarkwa-cassava-plantain-soil-metals">Accumulation of Heavy Metals and Metalloid in Foodstuffs from Agricultural Soils around Tarkwa Area in Ghana, and Associated Human Health Risks</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health (2015)</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/borteysam2015-tarkwa-cassava-plantain-soil-metals">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/orisakwe2012-owerri-food-crops-fruits-metals|5]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Orisakwe OE, Nduka JK, Amadi CN, Dike DO, Bede O · 2012</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/orisakwe2012-owerri-food-crops-fruits-metals">Heavy metals health risk assessment for population via consumption of food crops and fruits in Owerri, South Eastern, Nigeria</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Chemistry Central Journal 2012, 6:77</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/orisakwe2012-owerri-food-crops-fruits-metals">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</li>
<li>
<strong>Main drivers:</strong>

Farm location near mining and polluted river water, and ripening with calcium carbide, which raised arsenic in one study.<sup class="cite">[[sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops|2]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Adjei-Mensah R, Ofori H, Tortoe C, Johnson PT, Aryee D, Frimpong SK · 2021</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops">Effect of home processing methods on the levels of heavy metal contaminants in four food crops grown in and around two mining towns in Ghana</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Toxicology Reports 8 (2021) 1830–1838</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/borteysam2015-tarkwa-cassava-plantain-soil-metals|4]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Bortey-Sam N, Nakayama SMM, Akoto O, Ikenaka Y, Fobil JN, Baidoo E, Mizukawa H, Ishizuka M · 2015</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/borteysam2015-tarkwa-cassava-plantain-soil-metals">Accumulation of Heavy Metals and Metalloid in Foodstuffs from Agricultural Soils around Tarkwa Area in Ghana, and Associated Human Health Risks</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health (2015)</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/borteysam2015-tarkwa-cassava-plantain-soil-metals">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/mode2026-calcium-carbide-ripening-climacteric-fruits|6]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Mode AM, Magaji UF, Babatunde MS, Dandare A, Dabai IA, Dandare SU · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/mode2026-calcium-carbide-ripening-climacteric-fruits">Effects of Chemical Ripening With Calcium Carbide on Nutritional Composition, Antioxidant Capacity and Heavy Metal Accumulation in Climacteric Fruits</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">International Journal of Food Science 2026:7226409</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/mode2026-calcium-carbide-ripening-climacteric-fruits">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</li>
<li>
<strong>Practical framing:</strong>

Ask for lot lead results on the edible pulp, fresh weight, with a limit well below 100 µg/kg.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/eu-2023-915-contaminants-maximum-levels|3]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">European Commission · 2023</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/eu-2023-915-contaminants-maximum-levels">Commission Regulation (EU) 2023/915 of 25 April 2023 on maximum levels for certain contaminants in food and repealing Regulation (EC) No 1881/2006</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Official Journal of the European Union</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/eu-2023-915-contaminants-maximum-levels">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</li>
</ul>

<a id="decision-summary"></a>
## Plantain overview

<a id="hmi-ing-004"></a>
<a id="which-contamination-concerns-are-supported-for-this-ingredient-and-its-defined-forms"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-005"></a>
<a id="which-sourcing-or-production-decisions-deserve-priority-on-the-available-evidence"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-006"></a>
<a id="which-evidence-gaps-most-limit-those-decisions"></a>

Plantain has little monitoring data for metals, and the evidence that exists points in two directions. Plantain submitted to WHO GEMS/Food was mostly low: three cooked plantain samples from the WHO African region in 2018 had lead of 5 µg/kg or less and no detectable cadmium, mercury or arsenic, and four of five fresh plantain samples from the Americas in 2014–2016 had 1.5 µg/kg lead or less than detection limits of 1–5 µg/kg.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> The exception was one imported fresh plantain in 2016 at 174 µg/kg lead, above the 100 µg/kg limit that Codex and the EU apply to fruit.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/eu-2023-915-contaminants-maximum-levels|3]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">European Commission · 2023</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/eu-2023-915-contaminants-maximum-levels">Commission Regulation (EU) 2023/915 of 25 April 2023 on maximum levels for certain contaminants in food and repealing Regulation (EC) No 1881/2006</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Official Journal of the European Union</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/eu-2023-915-contaminants-maximum-levels">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/codex-cxs-193-1995|7]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Codex Alimentarius Commission · 1995</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/codex-cxs-193-1995">General Standard for Contaminants and Toxins in Food and Feed (CXS 193-1995)</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Codex Alimentarius (Joint FAO/WHO Food Standards Programme)</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/codex-cxs-193-1995">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

Plantain grown beside rivers used for illegal gold and diamond mining in Ghana measured far higher. Raw peeled pulp from farms at Obuasi and Akwatia averaged 1,020 and 1,110 µg/kg lead and 120–130 µg/kg mercury in 2019, on a basis the paper does not state but that appears to be the wet pulp.<sup class="cite">[[sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops|2]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Adjei-Mensah R, Ofori H, Tortoe C, Johnson PT, Aryee D, Frimpong SK · 2021</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops">Effect of home processing methods on the levels of heavy metal contaminants in four food crops grown in and around two mining towns in Ghana</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Toxicology Reports 8 (2021) 1830–1838</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Plantain from farms around the Tarkwa gold mines, sampled in 2012, had a geometric mean of only 7 µg/kg lead, so a mining district alone does not predict high lead.<sup class="cite">[[sources/borteysam2015-tarkwa-cassava-plantain-soil-metals|4]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Bortey-Sam N, Nakayama SMM, Akoto O, Ikenaka Y, Fobil JN, Baidoo E, Mizukawa H, Ishizuka M · 2015</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/borteysam2015-tarkwa-cassava-plantain-soil-metals">Accumulation of Heavy Metals and Metalloid in Foodstuffs from Agricultural Soils around Tarkwa Area in Ghana, and Associated Human Health Risks</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health (2015)</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/borteysam2015-tarkwa-cassava-plantain-soil-metals">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Ripening can add arsenic: in a Nigerian experiment, plantain ripened with calcium carbide had 5,930–9,940 µg/kg total arsenic against 1,640 µg/kg when ripened naturally, although that study’s arsenic levels are far above all other plantain data.<sup class="cite">[[sources/mode2026-calcium-carbide-ripening-climacteric-fruits|6]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Mode AM, Magaji UF, Babatunde MS, Dandare A, Dabai IA, Dandare SU · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/mode2026-calcium-carbide-ripening-climacteric-fruits">Effects of Chemical Ripening With Calcium Carbide on Nutritional Composition, Antioxidant Capacity and Heavy Metal Accumulation in Climacteric Fruits</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">International Journal of Food Science 2026:7226409</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/mode2026-calcium-carbide-ripening-climacteric-fruits">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

For a buyer, the supported priority is lead, measured on the edible pulp on a stated fresh-weight basis with a method that can see well below 100 µg/kg, together with the farm area where the plantain grew.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/eu-2023-915-contaminants-maximum-levels|3]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">European Commission · 2023</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/eu-2023-915-contaminants-maximum-levels">Commission Regulation (EU) 2023/915 of 25 April 2023 on maximum levels for certain contaminants in food and repealing Regulation (EC) No 1881/2006</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Official Journal of the European Union</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/eu-2023-915-contaminants-maximum-levels">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/colombiaminsalud2013-resolucion-4506-contaminants|8]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Ministerio de Salud y Proteccion Social · 2013</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/colombiaminsalud2013-resolucion-4506-contaminants">Resolucion Numero 4506 de 2013: niveles maximos de contaminantes en alimentos</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Ministerio de Salud y Proteccion Social</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/colombiaminsalud2013-resolucion-4506-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> In the one study that tested household cooking, boiling and frying left lead at 40–70 µg/kg from about 1,000 µg/kg in the raw pulp, a change in concentration rather than a measured removal.<sup class="cite">[[sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops|2]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Adjei-Mensah R, Ofori H, Tortoe C, Johnson PT, Aryee D, Frimpong SK · 2021</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops">Effect of home processing methods on (2021) 1830–1838</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>



<a id="ingredient-identity-and-scope"></a>
## What counts as plantain

<a id="hmi-ing-001"></a>
<a id="what-commodity-biological-species-edible-part-and-commercial-forms-does-this-page-cover"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-002"></a>
<a id="which-processing-states-and-derivatives-are-distinct-materials-rather-than-synonyms"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-003"></a>
<a id="what-evidence-can-be-transferred-between-those-materials-and-what-requires-a-separate-answer"></a>

This page covers plantain, the starchy cooking banana (Musa, often written Musa × paradisiaca), eaten cooked or as chips.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops|2]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Adjei-Mensah R, Ofori H, Tortoe C, Johnson PT, Aryee D, Frimpong SK · 2021</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops">Effect of home processing methods on the levels of heavy metal contaminants in four food crops grown in and around two mining towns in Ghana</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Toxicology Reports 8 (2021) 1830–1838</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> It does not cover the sweet dessert banana, which has its own page, and no banana value is used here. The herb also called plantain, Plantago (ribwort or narrowleaf plantain), is a different plant used in teas and herbal products, so its results are excluded.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/kowalska2021-metals-herbs-spices-tea-coffee-poland|9]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Kowalska G · 2021</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/kowalska2021-metals-herbs-spices-tea-coffee-poland">The Safety Assessment of Toxic Metals in Commonly Used Herbs, Spices, Tea, and Coffee in Poland</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/kowalska2021-metals-herbs-spices-tea-coffee-poland">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

Mixed dishes are also outside this page. A Nigerian survey reported metals in "beans with plantain", but the plantain’s share of that dish cannot be separated from the beans.<sup class="cite">[[sources/iyabo2015-ekiti-staple-foods-metals|10]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Iyabo OO, Ogundiran MB, Adebayo OL · 2015</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/iyabo2015-ekiti-staple-foods-metals">Toxic and Essential Metals in Staple Foods Commonly Consumed by Students in Ekiti State, South West, Nigeria</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">International Journal of Chemistry</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/iyabo2015-ekiti-staple-foods-metals">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> A Colombian study listed "Musa × paradisiaca" among local fruits without saying whether it meant plantain or banana, and its plant concentrations sit in a supplement the library does not hold.<sup class="cite">[[sources/authors2023-health-risk-assessment-for-human-exposure-to-heavy|11]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Unknown authors · 2023</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/authors2023-health-risk-assessment-for-human-exposure-to-heavy">Health Risk Assessment for Human Exposure to Heavy Metals</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Peer-reviewed article</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/authors2023-health-risk-assessment-for-human-exposure-to-heavy">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

Each source drawer identifies methods and overlapping samples. No matched reference or pooled distribution is inferred.</p></div></details><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure" data-baseline-fallback id="hmi-reference-hmi-pooled-reference-v2:plantain-Pb-cooked:9b260752b3be"><summary>HMI plantain Pb reference (Cooked, as eaten) · 1 sampling family</summary><div data-baseline-reference-template="hmi-pooled-reference-v2:plantain-Pb-cooked:9b260752b3be"><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Reference and scope</p><p>HMI plantain Pb reference (Cooked, as eaten) · 1 sampling family. Cooked plantain as consumed, wet weight, µg/kg; no moisture or cooking conversion. Distribution of subgroup median concentration values.</p><div class="hmi-drawer-table"><table><thead><tr><th scope="col">Reference (µg/kg)</th><th scope="col">Q1</th><th scope="col">Median</th><th scope="col">Q3</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>Primary HMI reference</td><td>3</td><td>3</td><td>3</td></tr><tr><td>Alternative weighting</td><td>3</td><td>3</td><td>3</td></tr></tbody></table></div><p>1 reference units; 1 sampling family. Counts describe evidence units, not independent studies or certainty.</p><div class="hmi-drawer-table"><table><thead><tr><th scope="col">Contributing family</th><th scope="col">Reference units</th><th scope="col">Weight</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>WHO GEMS/Food</td><td>1</td><td>100%</td></tr></tbody></table></div><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Methods</p><p>HMI pools WHO GEMS/Food plantain records as WHO-region × year medians for one basis (Cooked plantain as consumed, wet weight). Non-detects stay as zero-to-limit intervals. Means, ranges, maxima and results on another basis never enter.</p><p>Inverse weighted empirical CDF; midpoint at exact cumulative-weight boundaries. At least four reference units and a definitely positive Q1–Q3 spread are required. This is a display eligibility rule, not statistical validation.</p><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Limitations</p><p>GEMS/Food is the only family with individual plantain observations in the evidence library, and it holds very few plantain records; regions are reporting regions, not growing areas. Concentration is per weight of the prepared food; no moisture or mass-balance data, so concentration change mixes metal loss with water gain/loss. <a id="sources-and-contamination-pathways"></a>
## How metals reach plantain

<a id="hmi-ing-010"></a>
<a id="what-evidence-supports-root-uptake-surface-deposition-feed-transfer-or-other-biological-pathways"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-011"></a>
<a id="what-contamination-can-arise-from-agricultural-inputs-harvesting-processing-equipment-or-packaging"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-012"></a>
<a id="which-source-attribution-claims-are-measured-modelled-inferred-or-unresolved"></a>

The plantain studies point to soil, river water and dust in mining areas as the main sources. In Ghana, farms beside rivers used for illegal small-scale mining produced plantain pulp with about 1 mg/kg lead and 0.12–0.13 mg/kg mercury.<sup class="cite">[[sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops|2]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Adjei-Mensah R, Ofori H, Tortoe C, Johnson PT, Aryee D, Frimpong SK · 2021</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops">Effect of home processing methods on the levels of heavy metal contaminants in four food crops grown in and around two mining towns in Ghana</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Toxicology Reports 8 (2021) 1830–1838</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Around Tarkwa, soil-to-plantain transfer was lowest for chromium and highest for nickel (mean factor 2.2, the only metal above 1), and transfer did not correlate with soil pH or organic matter.<sup class="cite">[[sources/borteysam2015-tarkwa-cassava-plantain-soil-metals|4]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Bortey-Sam N, Nakayama SMM, Akoto O, Ikenaka Y, Fobil JN, Baidoo E, Mizukawa H, Ishizuka M · 2015</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/borteysam2015-tarkwa-cassava-plantain-soil-metals">Accumulation of Heavy Metals and Metalloid in Foodstuffs from Agricultural Soils around Tarkwa Area in Ghana, and Associated Human Health Risks</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health (2015)</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/borteysam2015-tarkwa-cassava-plantain-soil-metals">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

Arsenic may also arrive from the air. The Tarkwa authors linked arsenic in plantain, an aerial fruit, to wind-borne arsenic from ore roasting rather than to soil uptake, an explanation they did not test.<sup class="cite">[[sources/borteysam2015-tarkwa-cassava-plantain-soil-metals|4]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Bortey-Sam N, Nakayama SMM, Akoto O, Ikenaka Y, Fobil JN, Baidoo E, Mizukawa H, Ishizuka M · 2015</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/borteysam2015-tarkwa-cassava-plantain-soil-metals">Accumulation of Heavy Metals and Metalloid in Foodstuffs from Agricultural Soils around Tarkwa Area in Ghana, and Associated Human Health Risks</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health (2015)</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/borteysam2015-tarkwa-cassava-plantain-soil-metals">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Plantain is eaten peeled, and the Ghanaian study washed and peeled every sample before analysis, so none of the measured values includes the peel.<sup class="cite">[[sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops|2]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Adjei-Mensah R, Ofori H, Tortoe C, Johnson PT, Aryee D, Frimpong SK · 2021</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops">Effect of home processing methods on the levels of heavy metal contaminants in four food crops grown in and around two mining towns in Ghana</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Toxicology Reports 8 (2021) 1830–1838</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

Contamination can also be added after harvest. The technical calcium carbide used to ripen fruit in a Nigerian experiment contained 21.75 mg/kg arsenic and 0.881 mg/kg lead, and plantain ripened with it had more arsenic than plantain ripened naturally.<sup class="cite">[[sources/mode2026-calcium-carbide-ripening-climacteric-fruits|6]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Mode AM, Magaji UF, Babatunde MS, Dandare A, Dabai IA, Dandare SU · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/mode2026-calcium-carbide-ripening-climacteric-fruits">Effects of Chemical Ripening With Calcium Carbide on Nutritional Composition, Antioxidant Capacity and Heavy Metal Accumulation in Climacteric Fruits</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">International Journal of Food Science 2026:7226409</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/mode2026-calcium-carbide-ripening-climacteric-fruits">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Bortey-Sam N, Nakayama SMM, Akoto O, Ikenaka Y, Fobil JN, Baidoo E, Mizukawa H, Ishizuka M · 2015</span><a <details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="is-plantain-from-mining-areas-always-higher-in-metals" data-anchor="is-plantain-from-mining-areas-always-higher-in-metals" data-question="Is plantain from mining areas always higher in metals?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>Is plantain from mining areas always higher in metals?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

No. Plantain from farms around the Tarkwa gold mines had a geometric mean of 7 µg/kg lead and 1 µg/kg mercury in 2012.<sup class="cite">[[sources/borteysam2015-tarkwa-cassava-plantain-soil-metals|4]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Bortey-Sam N, Nakayama SMM, Akoto O, Ikenaka Y, Fobil JN, Baidoo E, Mizukawa H, Ishizuka M · 2015</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/borteysam2015-tarkwa-cassava-plantain-soil-metals">Accumulation of Heavy Metals and Metalloid in Foodstuffs from Agricultural Soils around Tarkwa Area in Ghana, and Associated Human Health Risks</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health (2015)</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/borteysam2015-tarkwa-cassava-plantain-soil-metals">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Plantain from farms on rivers used for illegal mining at Obuasi and Akwatia had about 1,000 µg/kg lead and 120–130 µg/kg mercury in 2019.<sup class="cite">[[sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops|2]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Adjei-Mensah R, Ofori H, Tortoe C, Johnson PT, Aryee D, Frimpong SK · 2021</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops">Effect of home processing methods on the levels of heavy metal contaminants in four food crops grown in and around two mining towns in Ghana</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Toxicology Reports 8 (2021) 1830–1838</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> The studies differ in year, basis and method, so the comparison shows a range of outcomes rather than a rule.

</div>
</details>

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="why-is-nickel-so-high-in-plantain" data-anchor="why-is-nickel-so-high-in-plantain" data-question="Why is nickel so high in plantain?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>Why is nickel so high in plantain?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

Nickel was the one metal that plantain took up from soil more readily than the soil held it: the Tarkwa soil-to-plantain factor averaged 2.2.<sup class="cite">[[sources/borteysam2015-tarkwa-cassava-plantain-soil-metals|4]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Bortey-Sam N, Nakayama SMM, Akoto O, Ikenaka Y, Fobil JN, Baidoo E, Mizukawa H, Ishizuka M · 2015</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/borteysam2015-tarkwa-cassava-plantain-soil-metals">Accumulation of Heavy Metals and Metalloid in Foodstuffs from Agricultural Soils around Tarkwa Area in Ghana, and Associated Human Health Risks</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health (2015)</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/borteysam2015-tarkwa-cassava-plantain-soil-metals">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Plantain there had 3,600 µg/kg nickel, and Owerri plantain had 1,000 µg/kg on a dry-weight basis.<sup class="cite">[[sources/borteysam2015-tarkwa-cassava-plantain-soil-metals|4]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Bortey-Sam N, Nakayama SMM, Akoto O, Ikenaka Y, Fobil JN, Baidoo E, Mizukawa H, Ishizuka M · 2015</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/borteysam2015-tarkwa-cassava-plantain-soil-metals">Accumulation of Heavy Metals and Metalloid in Foodstuffs from Agricultural Soils around Tarkwa Area in Ghana, and Associated Human Health Risks</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health (2015)</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/borteysam2015-tarkwa-cassava-plantain-soil-metals">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/orisakwe2012-owerri-food-crops-fruits-metals|5]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Orisakwe OE, Nduka JK, Amadi CN, Dike DO, Bede O · 2012</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/orisakwe2012-owerri-food-crops-fruits-metals">Heavy metals health risk assessment for population via consumption of food crops and fruits in Owerri, South Eastern, Nigeria</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Chemistry Central Journal 2012, 6:77</span><a class="cite-card-review" <a id="processing-effects-and-derivatives"></a>
## Cooking and processing

<a id="hmi-ing-016"></a>
<a id="how-do-specified-processing-or-preparation-steps-change-the-measured-metal-endpoints"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-017"></a>
<a id="how-do-derivatives-concentrates-extracts-and-fractions-differ-from-their-parent-ingredient"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-018"></a>
<a id="do-changes-reflect-removal-redistribution-moisture-or-yield-change-dilution-or-altered-species-or-availability"></a>

Only one study measured household processing of plantain, and it gives within-study comparisons from the same samples.<sup class="cite">[[sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops|2]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Adjei-Mensah R, Ofori H, Tortoe C, Johnson PT, Aryee D, Frimpong SK · 2021</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops">Effect of home processing methods on the levels of heavy metal contaminants in four food crops grown in and around two mining towns in Ghana</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Toxicology Reports 8 (2021) 1830–1838</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Boiling and frying lowered lead in peeled pulp from 1,020–1,110 µg/kg to 40–70 µg/kg at both towns, while roasting left 130 µg/kg at Obuasi and 750 µg/kg at Akwatia.<sup class="cite">[[sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops|2]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Adjei-Mensah R, Ofori H, Tortoe C, Johnson PT, Aryee D, Frimpong SK · 2021</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops">Effect of home processing methods on the levels of heavy metal contaminants in four food crops grown in and around two mining towns in Ghana</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Toxicology Reports 8 (2021) 1830–1838</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Mercury fell from 130 to 40–50 µg/kg after boiling or frying of Akwatia plantain, but changed little at Obuasi or after roasting.<sup class="cite">[[sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops|2]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Adjei-Mensah R, Ofori H, Tortoe C, Johnson PT, Aryee D, Frimpong SK · 2021</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops">Effect of home processing methods on the levels of heavy metal contaminants in four food crops grown in and around two mining towns in Ghana</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Toxicology Reports 8 (2021) 1830–1838</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

These are changes in concentration on a basis the paper does not state, without moisture or mass-balance data, so they do not show how much metal left the food.<sup class="cite">[[sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops|2]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Adjei-Mensah R, Ofori H, Tortoe C, Johnson PT, Aryee D, Frimpong SK · 2021</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops">Effect of home processing methods on the levels of heavy metal contaminants in four food crops grown in and around two mining towns in Ghana</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Toxicology Reports 8 (2021) 1830–1838</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Arsenic changes sit at the paper’s 0.01 mg/kg reporting step and cannot be distinguished.<sup class="cite">[[sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops|2]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Adjei-Mensah R, Ofori H, Tortoe C, Johnson PT, Aryee D, Frimpong SK · 2021</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops">Effect of home processing methods on the levels of heavy metal contaminants in four food crops grown in and around two mining towns in Ghana</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Toxicology Reports 8 (2021) 1830–1838</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Plantain chips, a common processed form, had 0.75 µg/kg inorganic arsenic in the single monitoring record, just above its 0.66 µg/kg detection limit.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

Ripening is the other measured step. Plantain ripened with 10 or 30 g of calcium carbide per kg of fruit had 5,930 and 9,940 µg/kg total arsenic against 1,640 µg/kg in naturally ripened fruit from the same bunch, significant increases in the authors’ analysis.<sup class="cite">[[sources/mode2026-calcium-carbide-ripening-climacteric-fruits|6]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Mode AM, Magaji UF, Babatunde MS, Dandare A, Dabai IA, Dandare SU · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/mode2026-calcium-carbide-ripening-climacteric-fruits">Effects of Chemical Ripening With Calcium Carbide on Nutritional Composition, Antioxidant Capacity and Heavy Metal Accumulation in Climacteric Fruits</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">International Journal of Food Science 2026:7226409</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/mode2026-calcium-carbide-ripening-climacteric-fruits">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Lead rose to 143–183 µg/kg in the carbide groups, but the natural-ripening lead value is printed identically to the mango control, so that comparison is not used; cadmium stayed at 1–3 µg/kg without a significant change.<sup class="cite">[[sources/mode2026-calcium-carbide-ripening-climacteric-fruits|6]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Mode AM, Magaji UF, Babatunde MS, Dandare A, Dabai IA, Dandare SU · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/mode2026-calcium-carbide-ripening-climacteric-fruits">Effects of Chemical Ripening With Calcium Carbide on Nutritional Composition, Antioxidant Capacity and Heavy Metal Accumulation in Climacteric Fruits</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">International Journal of Food Science 2026:7226409</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/mode2026-calcium-carbide-ripening-climacteric-fruits">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>



<a id="mitigation-options"></a>
## Mitigation from farm to plate

<a id="hmi-ing-019"></a>
<a id="which-prevention-mitigation-or-remediation-measures-have-been-evaluated-for-this-ingredient"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-020"></a>
<a id="under-what-conditions-at-which-stage-and-against-which-comparator-do-they-work-or-fail"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-021"></a>
<a id="what-evidence-supports-field-or-commercial-implementation-and-ongoing-verification"></a>

Controls for plantain act at the farm, in the kitchen and at the lot test. The only measured control is household cooking in one Ghanaian study, where boiling and frying gave much lower lead concentrations than raw pulp and roasting gave less change.<sup class="cite">[[sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops|2]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Adjei-Mensah R, Ofori H, Tortoe C, one controlled experiment in which carbide raised arsenic in plantain.<sup class="cite">[[sources/mode2026-calcium-carbide-ripening-climacteric-fruits|6]]<span class="cite-card"><span Linked analytes, repeated seasons and reports are not independent studies.</p><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Effects and comparators</p><div class="hmi-selected-result"><p><strong>Nickel</strong><strong>Transfer factor above 1 (observational)</strong><span class="hmi-comparison-detail">Soil-to-plantain bioconcentration factor</span><span class="hmi-comparison-detail">Plantain versus farm soil</span><span class="hmi-comparison-detail hmi-row-note">Dry weight ratio</span><span class="hmi-comparison-detail hmi-row-note"><strong>Context</strong> · No supported numerical treatment contrast is retained for this finding. A direction, market association, source-selection strategy or guidance statement alone does not establish a percentage change.</span></p><p><strong>Total chromium</strong><strong>Lowest transfer from soil (observational)</strong><span class="hmi-comparison-detail">Soil-to-plantain bioconcentration factor</span><span class="hmi-comparison-detail">Plantain versus farm soil</span><span class="hmi-comparison-detail hmi-row-note">Dry weight ratio</span><span class="hmi-comparison-detail hmi-row-note"><strong>Context</strong> · No supported numerical treatment contrast is retained for this finding. A direction, market association, source-selection strategy or guidance statement alone does not establish a percentage change.</span></p></div><p>Plantain versus the topsoil of the same farms.</p><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">How magnitude is classified</p><p>HMI editorial magnitude bands: Low is a change greater than 0% and below 25%; Moderate is 25% to below 50%; High is 50% or more, relative to that control’s own comparator. A range spanning bands retains both labels; a qualitative label has no implied percentage.</p><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Control in context</p><p>Soil-to-plantain transfer factors were lowest for chromium and highest for nickel (mean 2.2), the only metal above 1; soil pH and organic matter did not explain transfer.</p><div class="hmi-drawer-table"><table><thead><tr><th scope="col">Context</th><th scope="col">Selected control</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>Material</td><td>32 plantain samples and farm soils, Tarkwa, Ghana (June 2012)</td></tr><tr><td>Stage</td><td>cultivation</td></tr><tr><td>Audience</td><td>Ingredient suppliers · Brands</td></tr><tr><td>Period</td><td>As reported</td></tr><tr><td>Conditions</td><td>Gold-mining area farms; one season.</td></tr><tr><td>Tested scale</td><td>Field survey</td></tr><tr><td>Sample units</td><td>Source sampling units; processed portions cut from the same raw samples are not independent.</td></tr><tr><td>Trade-offs</td><td>Moisture, oil uptake, nutrients and cost not quantified.</td></tr><tr><td>Verification</td><td>Confirm with lot-specific results on the edible pulp, fresh weight, with an adequate quantification limit.</td></tr></tbody></table></div><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Design, applicability and operating conditions</p><p>Observational field survey. <a id="finished-product-and-exposure-implications"></a>
## Exposure from plantain

<a id="hmi-ing-031"></a>
<a id="how-do-inclusion-rate-processing-yield-preparation-and-other-ingredients-affect-a-finished-product-estimate"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-032"></a>
<a id="how-do-consumption-patterns-and-intended-populations-affect-dietary-exposure-interpretation"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-033"></a>
<a id="what-conclusions-require-finished-product-measurements-or-a-separate-exposure-assessment"></a>

Plantain is a staple in parts of West Africa, so its metal content matters more there than its small share of most Western diets. The Ghanaian processing study assumed average consumption of 101.8 kg of plantain per person per year.<sup class="cite">[[sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops|2]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Adjei-Mensah R, Ofori H, Tortoe C, Johnson PT, Aryee D, Frimpong SK · 2021</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops">Effect of home processing methods on the levels of heavy metal contaminants in four food crops grown in and around two mining towns in Ghana</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Toxicology Reports 8 (2021) 1830–1838</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> No source in the ledger estimates plantain’s share of dietary metal intake in a way that can be checked: the Ghanaian study’s intake and hazard tables do not follow from its own concentration table.<sup class="cite">[[sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops|2]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Adjei-Mensah R, Ofori H, Tortoe C, Johnson PT, Aryee D, Frimpong SK · 2021</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops">Effect of home processing methods on the levels of heavy metal contaminants in four food crops grown in and around two mining towns in Ghana</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Toxicology Reports 8 (2021) 1830–1838</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

For most plantain eaten cooked, the monitoring results suggest little lead, cadmium, mercury or arsenic.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Where plantain grows beside mining-polluted rivers, the raw pulp was far above the 100 µg/kg fruit lead limit, and boiled or fried portions (40–70 µg/kg) still exceeded every monitoring result except the single 174 µg/kg import.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · <a id="requirements-evidence-assessment-and-updates"></a>
## Evidence review and remaining gaps

<a id="hmi-ing-034"></a>
<a id="which-primary-regulatory-instruments-apply-to-this-exact-ingredient-form-species-market-and-date"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-035"></a>
<a id="what-searches-eligibility-decisions-source-families-and-appraisal-underpin-the-answers-and-certainty-judgments"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-036"></a>
<a id="what-remains-unresolved-when-was-each-answer-reviewed-and-what-changed-in-this-version"></a>

This assessment covers every source record in the HMI library that is tagged to plantain or mentions it, every plantain row in WHO GEMS/Food, and library papers found by searching their text for plantain and its scientific name. Four studies had no source record and are proposed for addition, two of them checked against publisher PDFs supplied for this review; two other library papers measured only plantain leaves or pooled plantain with other vegetables and are not used.<sup class="cite">[[sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops|2]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span The evidence is thin: five sampling families, no total diet study, very few monitoring records and no cultivar comparisons.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Total diet studies and monitoring from Nigeria, Ghana, Cameroon, Côte d’Ivoire, Uganda and the plantain-eating countries of Latin America are the main gaps.

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="how-do-heavy-metals-get-into-plantain" data-anchor="how-do-heavy-metals-get-into-plantain" data-question="How do heavy metals get into plantain?">

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="which-types-of-plantain-have-the-lowest-levels" data-anchor="which-types-of-plantain-have-the-lowest-levels" data-question="Which types of plantain have the lowest levels?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>Which types of plantain have the lowest levels?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

No study in the ledger compares plantain cultivars. By form, cooked plantain and most fresh plantain in monitoring were lowest for lead, at 5 µg/kg or below.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="which-growing-regions-produce-plantain-with-the-lowest-levels" data-anchor="which-growing-regions-produce-plantain-with-the-lowest-levels" data-question="Which growing regions produce plantain with the lowest levels?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>Which growing regions produce plantain with the lowest levels?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

The evidence cannot rank regions. <summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>Do foods made from plantain also contain heavy metals?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

The one plantain-chip record had 0.75 µg/kg inorganic arsenic, just above its detection limit.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> No study in the ledger measured metals in plantain flour.

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="are-there-legal-limits-for-heavy-metals-in-plantain" data-anchor="are-there-legal-limits-for-heavy-metals-in-plantain" data-question="Are there legal limits for heavy metals in plantain?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>Are there legal limits for heavy metals in plantain?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

Plantain falls under general fruit limits: lead 0.1 mg/kg in Codex, the EU and Colombia.<sup class="cite">[[sources/eu-2023-915-contaminants-maximum-levels|3]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">European Commission · 2023</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/eu-2023-915-contaminants-maximum-levels">Commission Regulation (EU) 2023/915 of 25 April 2023 on maximum levels for certain contaminants in food and repealing Regulation (EC) No 1881/2006</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Official Journal of the European Union</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/eu-2023-915-contaminants-maximum-levels">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/codex-cxs-193-1995|7]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Codex Alimentarius Commission · 1995</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/codex-cxs-193-1995">General Standard for Contaminants and Toxins in Food and Feed (CXS 193-1995)</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Codex Alimentarius (Joint FAO/WHO Food Standards Programme)</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/codex-cxs-193-1995">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/colombiaminsalud2013-resolucion-4506-contaminants|8]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Ministerio de Salud y Proteccion Social · 2013</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/colombiaminsalud2013-resolucion-4506-contaminants">Resolucion Numero 4506 de 2013: niveles maximos de contaminantes en alimentos</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Ministerio de Salud y Proteccion Social</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/colombiaminsalud2013-resolucion-4506-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> For cadmium the EU sets 0.020 mg/kg for bananas and 0.050 mg/kg for most other fruit, and Colombia sets 0.050 mg/kg; no limit names plantain itself.<sup class="cite">[[sources/eu-2023-915-contaminants-maximum-levels|3]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span <details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="can-cooking-or-processing-reduce-metals-in-plantain" data-anchor="can-cooking-or-processing-reduce-metals-in-plantain" data-question="Can cooking or processing reduce metals in plantain?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>Can cooking or processing reduce metals in plantain?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

In one Ghanaian study, boiling and frying gave lead concentrations of 40–70 µg/kg from about 1,000 µg/kg raw, while roasting changed lead less.<sup class="cite">[[sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops|2]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Adjei-Mensah R, Ofori H, Tortoe C, Johnson PT, Aryee D, Frimpong SK · 2021</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops">Effect of home processing methods on the levels of heavy metal contaminants in four food crops grown in and around two mining towns in Ghana</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Toxicology Reports 8 (2021) 1830–1838</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> The study did not measure moisture or weigh the metal lost, so how much lead left the food is unknown.<sup class="cite">[[sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops|2]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Adjei-Mensah R, Ofori H, Tortoe C, Johnson PT, Aryee D, Frimpong SK · 2021</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops">Effect of home processing methods on the levels of heavy metal contaminants in four food crops grown in and around two mining towns in Ghana</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Toxicology Reports 8 (2021) 1830–1838</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</div>
</details>

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="is-the-arsenic-in-plantain-the-toxic-inorganic-form" data-anchor="is-the-arsenic-in-plantain-the-toxic-inorganic-form" data-question="Is the arsenic in plantain the toxic inorganic form?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>Is the arsenic in plantain the toxic inorganic form?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

Almost every plantain arsenic result is total arsenic, so the form is unknown.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants <details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="does-ripening-plantain-with-calcium-carbide-add-heavy-metals" data-anchor="does-ripening-plantain-with-calcium-carbide-add-heavy-metals" data-question="Does ripening plantain with calcium carbide add heavy metals?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>Does ripening plantain with calcium carbide add heavy metals?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

In the one experiment that tested it, yes for arsenic: carbide-ripened plantain had 5,930–9,940 µg/kg total arsenic against 1,640 µg/kg when ripened naturally, and the carbide itself contained 21.75 mg/kg arsenic.<sup class="cite">[[sources/mode2026-calcium-carbide-ripening-climacteric-fruits|6]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Mode AM, Magaji UF, Babatunde MS, Dandare A, Dabai IA, Dandare SU · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/mode2026-calcium-carbide-ripening-climacteric-fruits">Effects of Chemical Ripening With Calcium Carbide on Nutritional Composition, Antioxidant Capacity and Heavy Metal Accumulation in Climacteric Fruits</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">International Journal of Food Science 2026:7226409</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/mode2026-calcium-carbide-ripening-climacteric-fruits">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Cadmium did not change significantly, and the study’s arsenic levels are far above other plantain data, so the size of the effect is uncertain.<sup class="cite">[[sources/mode2026-calcium-carbide-ripening-climacteric-fruits|6]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Mode AM, Magaji UF, Babatunde MS, Dandare A, Dabai IA, Dandare SU · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/mode2026-calcium-carbide-ripening-climacteric-fruits">Effects of Chemical Ripening With Calcium Carbide on Nutritional Composition, Antioxidant Capacity and Heavy Metal Accumulation in Climacteric Fruits</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">International Journal of Food Science 2026:7226409</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/mode2026-calcium-carbide-ripening-climacteric-fruits">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</div>
</details>

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="is-banana-lower-in-metals-than-plantain" data-anchor="is-banana-lower-in-metals-than-plantain" data-question="Is banana lower in metals than plantain?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>Is banana lower in metals than plantain?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

They are different fruits, and this page uses no banana values. In the one study that measured both by the same method, in Owerri, banana had more lead (0.46 mg/kg) and plantain more cadmium and nickel, so neither was lower overall.<sup class="cite">[[sources/orisakwe2012-owerri-food-crops-fruits-metals|5]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Orisakwe OE, Nduka JK, Amadi CN, Dike DO, Bede O · 2012</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/orisakwe2012-owerri-food-crops-fruits-metals">Heavy metals health risk assessment for population via consumption of food crops and fruits in Owerri, South Eastern, Nigeria</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Chemistry Central Journal 2012, 6:77</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/orisakwe2012-owerri-food-crops-fruits-metals">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</div>
</details>

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="does-cooking-destroy-heavy-metals-in-plantain" data-anchor="does-cooking-destroy-heavy-metals-in-plantain" data-question="Does cooking destroy heavy metals in plantain?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>Does cooking destroy heavy metals in plantain?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

No; heat cannot destroy a metal. Cooking can change the concentration by moving water, oil or metal in or out of the food, which is what the Ghanaian study measured.<sup class="cite">[[sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops|2]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Adjei-Mensah R, Ofori H, Tortoe C, Johnson PT, Aryee D, Frimpong SK · 2021</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops">Effect of home processing methods on the levels of heavy metal contaminants in four food crops grown in and around two mining towns in Ghana</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Toxicology Reports 8 (2021) 1830–1838</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</div>
</details>

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="is-plantain-the-same-as-the-herb-called-plantain" data-anchor="is-plantain-the-same-as-the-herb-called-plantain" data-question="Is plantain the same as the herb called plantain?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>Is plantain the same as the herb called plantain?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

No. The herb is Plantago (ribwort or narrowleaf plantain), used in teas and herbal medicines, and its metal results are excluded from this page.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/kowalska2021-metals-herbs-spices-tea-coffee-poland|9]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Kowalska G · 2021</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/kowalska2021-metals-herbs-spices-tea-coffee-poland">The Safety Assessment of Toxic Metals in Commonly Used Herbs, Spices, Tea, and Coffee in Poland</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/kowalska2021-metals-herbs-spices-tea-coffee-poland">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</div>
</details>

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="does-growing-plantain-near-mining-raise-metal-levels" data-anchor="does-growing-plantain-near-mining-raise-metal-levels" data-question="Does growing plantain near mining raise metal levels?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>Does growing plantain near mining raise metal levels?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

It can. Plantain from farms on rivers used for illegal mining in Ghana was far above the fruit lead limit, but plantain from farms around the Tarkwa gold mines was low in lead.<sup class="cite">[[sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops|2]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Adjei-Mensah R, Ofori H, Tortoe C, Johnson PT, Aryee D, Frimpong SK · 2021</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops">Effect of home processing methods on the levels of heavy metal contaminants in four food crops grown in and around two mining towns in Ghana</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Toxicology Reports 8 (2021) 1830–1838</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/borteysam2015-tarkwa-cassava-plantain-soil-metals|4]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Bortey-Sam N, Nakayama SMM, Akoto O, Ikenaka Y, Fobil JN, Baidoo E, Mizukawa H, Ishizuka M · 2015</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/borteysam2015-tarkwa-cassava-plantain-soil-metals">Accumulation of Heavy Metals and Metalloid in Foodstuffs from Agricultural Soils around Tarkwa Area in Ghana, and Associated Human Health Risks</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health (2015)</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/borteysam2015-tarkwa-cassava-plantain-soil-metals">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</div>
</details>

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="does-plantain-contain-mercury" data-anchor="does-plantain-contain-mercury" data-question="Does plantain contain mercury?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>Does plantain contain mercury?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

Usually very little: monitoring found none above 4.2 µg/kg and Tarkwa plantain had 1 µg/kg.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/borteysam2015-tarkwa-cassava-plantain-soil-metals|4]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Bortey-Sam N, Nakayama SMM, Akoto O, Ikenaka Y, Fobil JN, Baidoo E, Mizukawa H, Ishizuka M · 2015</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/borteysam2015-tarkwa-cassava-plantain-soil-metals">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Plantain from Ghanaian mining-river farms had 120–130 µg/kg, which cooking did not reliably lower.<sup class="cite">[[sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops|2]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span in Ghana</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Toxicology Reports 8 (2021) 1830–1838</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</div>
</details>

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="what-should-a-plantain-lead-test-report" data-anchor="what-should-a-plantain-lead-test-report" data-question="What should a plantain lead test report?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>What should a plantain lead test report?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

The edible pulp, fresh weight, the laboratory’s quantification limit and the farm area.<sup class="cite">[[sources/eu-2023-915-contaminants-maximum-levels|3]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">European Commission · 2023</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/eu-2023-915-contaminants-maximum-levels">Commission Regulation (EU) 2023/915 of 25 April 2023 on maximum levels for certain contaminants in food and repealing Regulation (EC) No 1881/2006</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Official Journal of the European Union</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/eu-2023-915-contaminants-maximum-levels">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/colombiaminsalud2013-resolucion-4506-contaminants|8]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Ministerio de Salud y Proteccion Social · 2013</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/colombiaminsalud2013-resolucion-4506-contaminants">Resolucion Numero 4506 de 2013: niveles maximos de contaminantes en alimentos</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Ministerio de Salud y Proteccion Social</span><a class="cite-card-review"
